sections.h2: Seller costs set by Wisconsin law
sections.html:
State law hands a Wisconsin seller three obligations: the transfer fee on the deed, the recording cost for any paper the seller must file, and a condition report for the buyer. Commission, title charges and the year's property tax split are different. They come out of your contract and settlement statement.

Start by pricing the transfer fee. Wis. Stat. 77.22 puts it on the grantor, and it is paid to the register of deeds as the deed is recorded. Recording itself is a flat $30 under Wis. Stat. 59.43(2)(ag). The rest is negotiable, so have the closing agent write out an estimate before you sign.

Thirty cents is charged per $100 of value, and a leftover fraction of $100 is rounded up to a whole one.

"Value" is a defined term. Under Wis. Stat. 77.21(3), a conveyance that isn't a gift is valued at everything actually paid or promised, liens on the property included. Gifts, deeds for token consideration and exchanges are valued at an estimated open-market price. Land contracts use the principal the buyer promises to pay.

sections.h2: Seller charges and deadlines at a glance
sections.html:
Charge or dutyAmount or deadlineStatute
Transfer fee30 cents per $100 of value or fraction, owed by the grantorWis. Stat. 77.22(1)
Recording a deed$30 per documentWis. Stat. 59.43(2)(ag)
Copy of a recorded document$2 for page one, $1 for each further page, $1 extra to certifyWis. Stat. 59.43(2)(b)
Real estate condition report to buyerWithin 10 days after contract acceptanceWis. Stat. 709.02(1)
Mortgage payoff statement from lenderWithin 7 business days after a written request on residential propertyWis. Stat. 708.15(3)

Recording fees are payable in advance by whoever asks the register for the service.

Only conveyances that match a category in Wis. Stat. 77.25 escape the fee, and the deed itself must name the exemption. Homeowners most often run into these:

  • Passing by will, descent or survivorship.
  • Foreclosure deeds, and deeds in lieu, to a mortgage holder or land contract seller.
  • Sales for delinquent taxes or assessments.
  • A trustee's deed to a beneficiary with no real consideration.
  • A corrective or confirming deed for a conveyance already recorded, given for nominal, inadequate or no consideration.
  • A deed that merely gives or releases security for a debt not arising from a conveyance.
  • Condemnation, or real estate worth $1,000 or less.

A deed from a land contract seller is also exempt when the proper fee was paid at the time the land contract was recorded. Statute 77.256 bars a city, village, town or county from charging its own fee on an exempt conveyance.

The Department of Revenue's transfer return reports value, fee and any exemption, and the grantor and grantee both sign. Without a finished return and the fee, the register of deeds won't record the conveyance, except in the narrow no-return cases of Wis. Stat. 77.255.

The form is now filed through My Tax Account. Filers need no username or password and can file, view or amend a return. For ordinary sales the title company or attorney usually files it. If you sign a deed on your own, the department's RETR page has guides and the exemption list.

Wis. Stat. 77.24 divides the money: the county keeps 20 percent and the state gets the remainder. The department may later examine a return and assess more fee, or refund an overpayment, if the value was misreported or an exemption was claimed wrongly.

Sellers of property with one to four dwelling units owe the buyer a completed condition report inside 10 days of accepting an offer. The form, set out in Wis. Stat. 709.03, asks about structure, mechanical systems, environmental issues, wells, septic and storage tanks, taxes and special assessments, permits, and land use.

If the report is late, the buyer can back out within two business days after the 10 days run out and gets the deposit back. A seller who learned something before acceptance that alters an answer must send an amended report or an amendment inside the same 10 days. The form is not a warranty and doesn't replace inspections.

A few sellers are excused: a court-appointed fiduciary, such as a personal representative, who never occupied the property; an owner of a property that has never been inhabited; and any transfer exempt from the fee. The chapter covers sales, exchanges and land contracts.

Ask your lender in writing for a payoff statement. On a loan secured by residential property, the lender must send it within 7 business days. Under Wis. Stat. 708.15 the statement shows the payoff amount on its date and the information needed to compute it for the requested payoff date, such as the per diem interest, plus the payment cutoff time and where and how to pay.

The request can name a payoff date up to 30 days out, and an agent you authorize, such as the closing agent, may make it. On residential property a lender can't qualify the amount or say it may change before that date, which gives the closing agent a firm number. Ask early enough to fit your scheduled closing.

sections.h2: Questions to ask the closing agent
sections.html:
Get an itemized estimate before closing and compare each line with the amounts above. These questions catch most surprises:

  • What value is being reported on the transfer return, and does it include any lien being paid off?
  • Is any exemption being claimed, and under which subsection of Wis. Stat. 77.25?
  • What is the per diem on my mortgage, and through what payoff date is the statement good?
  • What is the balance on the property tax bill, and how is the current year prorated?
  • Which charges come from the contract, such as commission, title and repair credits, and which come from statute?
  • Has the condition report been delivered, and on what date?

For the tax balance, ask the county treasurer or the municipal treasurer that bills the parcel. The property tax bill names the office that collects. If you sell for cash as-is, many of these lines shrink, though the transfer fee, recording and your payoff still apply.

faqs.q: Who pays the real estate transfer fee in Wisconsin?
faqs.a: The seller does. Wis. Stat. 77.22 charges the grantor 30 cents per $100 of value, payable to the register of deeds at recording.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Wisconsin?
faqs.a: Recording runs a flat $30 per document under Wis. Stat. 59.43(2)(ag). Copies are $2 for page one and $1 for each added page, and certifying adds $1.

faqs.q: Is the transfer fee based on the sale price or the equity?
faqs.a: The sale price, not the equity. On a sale, value is the full consideration paid or to be paid, including any lien, so your mortgage balance doesn't lower the amount the fee is measured on.

faqs.q: When must I give the buyer the condition report?
faqs.a: Inside 10 days of acceptance. A buyer who misses that deadline can rescind during the next two business days and recover the deposit.

faqs.q: How long does my lender have to send a payoff statement?
faqs.a: Seven business days after it receives your written request, on a loan secured by residential property. The statement shows the payoff amount and the per diem interest.
